newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal should meet EMU deficit target - official.
newsitem.headline: Portugal should meet EMU deficit target - official.

text.p: Portugal is expected to meet the European Union's single currency deficit target next year whichever of the country's two estimates of economic growth are used, Emanuel Santos, director of the Finance Ministry's research team, said.

The Finance Ministry and the independent National Statistics Institute (INE) produce different calculations of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), mainly because of the way they calculate growth in the construction industry.
INE's GDP estimate is usually lower which implies a higher deficit as a percentage of GDP.

"The difference between the two measures adds up to a widening of the deficit (as a percentage of GDP) of 0.1 percentage points. That won't put the Maastricht convergence criteria in jeopardy (for 1997)," Santos told Reuters.
The government has forecast a 1997 deficit of 2.9 percent of GDP, just below the 3.0 percent ceiling set out in the Maastricht Treaty.
The deficit for 1996 is expected to be around 4.0 percent.
The 1997 budget proposal is based on total GDP of 17,669 billion escudos with a deficit of 512.8 billion.
INE does not publish forecasts and the last GDP figure it released was for 1995. It gave a provisional figure of 15,073 billion escudos, compared with the Finance Ministry's 15,576 billion.
If the 1995 differential of 503 billion escudos were applied to the government's 1997 GDP calculations, it would give a budget deficit of 2.99 percent, still below the 3.0 percent Maastricht goal.
Santos said the discrepancy between the two measurements had only arisen since 1995 when INE made alterations to the way it calculated growth, particularly in the construction industry.
Previously, the two institutions had used the same figure for GDP.
Santos said the Finance Ministry and the Bank of Portugal had expressed reservations about INE's new methods and a working group had been set up to study the question.
"The interests of the Finance Ministry would be better suited if there were a lower GDP figure because of the impact that would have on the contributions we make to the European Union," Santos said.
Most analysts believe Portugal has a reasonable chance of joining the single currency when it is formally launched in 1999.
